sources_considered.why: The randomized SHIELD-RT study reports actual acute-care outcomes and explains what was randomized.
The investigating university reports completed MASAI follow-up. The measured outcomes concern screening, not demonstrated mortality reduction.
The primary MASAI article was located, but read_page returned HTTP 403.
Official mortality data provide context about cancer's continuing burden. They do not attribute outcomes to AI.
Read for population trends; those trends do not isolate an AI contribution.

evidence_items.publisher: Journal of Clinical Oncology, indexed by PubMed
evidence_items.locator: Abstract, Conclusion; design and numerical results in Patients and methods and Results

receipt.public_excerpt: reduced acute care rates versus standard of care.

evidence_items.explanation: Among patients selected as high risk by machine learning, additional evaluations reduced acute-care visits during treatment from 22.3% to 12.3%. This challenges a zero-benefit reading, but randomization tested additional visits among AI-selected patients, not AI selection against selection without AI.

evidence_items.locator: Latest findings, first bullet; preceding paragraph dates completion of follow-up
evidence_items.explanation: MASAI supplies comparative evidence of better screening outcomes before the post. The reported interval-cancer counts do not themselves establish a reduction in deaths or suffering, and this release does not establish superiority statistically.

evidence_items.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence_items.explanation: These retrospective data concern a period before the post and document the continuing burden. They neither measure AI exposure nor show what mortality would have been without AI.

unresolved_gaps: No population estimate isolating AI's contribution to cancer mortality or suffering was established.
The strongest patient-care study found here does not isolate the incremental effect of AI selection from the additional clinical care.
The wording does not settle whether limited clinical benefits would count as changing cancer's toll.
A lack of demonstrated population benefit is not proof of no benefit.
